cues.text: A Reluctant Soldier's Conversion
Pachomius was born about the year 292 near Esneh in Upper Egypt, to parents who worshipped the old gods of the Nile.

At twenty he was seized for the army, one of many young Egyptians conscripted to serve the Emperor Constantine's campaigns, and shipped downriver under guard with other frightened recruits who had no idea what awaited them.
At the town of Latopolis, local Christians came to the riverbank and fed the prisoners, asking nothing in return — an act of ordinary charity Pachomius never forgot.
He resolved then, if God delivered him from the army, to give his own life to the God whose followers could love strangers so freely.
He kept that promise: discharged after brief service, he sought baptism and apprenticed himself to the hermit Palamon, who taught him to combine unceasing prayer with hard manual labor.
A Vision at Tabennisi
Hermits in the Egyptian desert of that age lived, for the most part, alone, meeting occasionally for prayer but withdrawing again into private struggle.
Pachomius stayed for a time at the deserted village of Tabennisi on the Nile's east bank.
He believed he received a vision there commanding him to remain and build not another hermitage but a monastery — a house where many could live the ascetic life together.
Palamon helped him raise the first cell around the year 320, and before long Pachomius's own elder brother John joined him, followed by others drawn to the same idea.

It was a genuinely new proposal: rather than each man wrestling alone in his own cave, monks would share meals, labor, and the hours of prayer, held together by a common rule rather than each hermit's private discipline.
A Rule for the Common Life
The move from solitary to shared life did not come easily even to those who wanted it — early companions, formed only in the eremitical ideal, chafed at meals in common and organized labor.
Pachomius met this with patience, taking on the heaviest and least attractive work himself so newcomers might grow gradually into the rhythm of community.
Out of this experience, he drew up what is generally recognized as the first written rule for cenobitic, or communal, monastic life.
It established a structured pattern of prayer, work, and common meals, teachable to hundreds rather than handed down from one hermit to one disciple.

The rule spread with startling speed: by the time of Pachomius's death, the monastery at Tabennisi had grown into eleven communities in all, nine for men and two for women, following his pattern along the Nile.
Father of a New Kind of Monk
Word of Pachomian monasticism traveled far beyond Egypt in Pachomius's own lifetime, carried by pilgrims and by his Rule.
It circulated in Greek and was translated into Latin in the early fifth century.
St. Anthony of Egypt , whose solitary combat in the desert had already made him famous, represented one great model of Christian asceticism — the hermit alone with God.
Pachomius, his younger contemporary, offered another, no less demanding but built for the many rather than the few.
Both models flowed, decades later, into the monastic legislation of St. Basil the Great in the East.
Still later, they flowed into the Rule St. Benedict of Nursia composed for the West, which owed a real, if indirect, debt to the discipline Pachomius worked out at Tabennisi two centuries before.
Legacy
Pachomius died, most likely of plague, around the year 346, having lived to see his improbable experiment become an established way of life for thousands.

He shows every Christian who has ever tried to build something larger than personal virtue — a parish, a family, a community of any kind — that holiness is rarely only a private matter between one soul and God.
It is also a patient, unglamorous work of learning to live well with others: sharing labor, bearing with the slow and the stubborn, building structures sturdy enough to outlast their founder.
The monk once thought only of surviving the army.
However unlikely it seemed, he now stands as the father of an entire way of Christian life.
It remains practiced, in spirit if not in every particular, wherever men and women vow to seek God not alone but together.
